title: AutoPower: Automated Few-Shot Architecture-Level Power Modeling by Power Group Decoupling
problem: Traditional analytical architecture-level power models are inaccurate; recent ML-based approaches require sufficient training data from known configurations, which is unrealistic for early-stage power estimation with limited design configurations.
method: AutoPower decouples power consumption into independent power groups (e.g., clock, SRAM, logic) and builds individual ML models for each group based on correlations with structural information available at the architecture level. Further decoupling within power groups creates multiple sub-models, enabling accurate few-shot learning with minimal training data.

title: Dilu: Enabling GPU Resourcing-on-Demand for Serverless DL Serving via Introspective Elasticity
problem: Serverless DL serving systems use coarse-grained static GPU allocation that produces 15-94% GPU fragmentation due to dynamic workload patterns; existing horizontal-only scaling cannot adapt GPU resource allocation fine-grainedly within a running DL function instance, degrading utilization and violating QoS.
method: Dilu introduces Introspective Elasticity (IE), a two-dimensional co-scaling mechanism combining vertical scaling (adjusting GPU resource allocation within a running DL task) and horizontal scaling (adding/removing instances). Dilu uses multi-factor profiling with efficient pruning search to characterize each DL function's GPU compute/memory sensitivity. A cross-layer scheduler applies resourcing-complementary principles to fill fragmented GPU capacity with compatible DL tasks. At runtime, an adaptive 2D co-scaling controller continuously monitors QoS signals and adjusts both per-instance GPU allocation and the number of instances to minimize fragmentation while meeting SLAs.

title: A Blocker-Tolerant mm-Wave Low-Noise Amplifier Utilizing Doherty Active Load Modulation for Linearity Enhancement
problem: Emerging mm-wave applications (massive MIMO, automotive radar, SATCOM-on-the-Move, AR/VR) require high-linearity receivers/LNAs to handle multiple concurrent signals or weak signals amid strong interferers. Conventional LNA designs optimize for noise at weak signals but cannot maintain linearity with strong blockers.
method: Blocker-tolerant mm-wave LNA leveraging Doherty active load modulation to enhance linearity across wide input power range. Doherty architecture dynamically adjusts gain vs. linearity trade-off, maintaining output power efficiency under strong blockers.

title: Efficient Memory Side-Channel Protection for Embedding Generation in Machine Learning
problem: Embedding table lookups in ML models (DLRMs, LLMs) leak sensitive input features (user IDs, token indices) through memory access patterns, making them vulnerable to side-channel attacks; protecting these accesses with conventional ORAM incurs prohibitive overhead due to the massive size of embedding tables.
method: The paper evaluates three protection strategies: (1) linear scan of the embedding table (accesses all rows, hiding which row is used); (2) ORAM protection with optimized implementation; and (3) Deep Hash Embedding (DHE), which replaces the table lookup entirely with a hash-based neural network computation that takes the embedding index as input and produces an embedding vector through compute rather than memory access, eliminating the memory access pattern. A hybrid scheme combines DHE for large embedding tables (where its compute cost is amortized) with linear scan for small tables, selected per table based on profiled break-even points.

title: Cayman: Custom Accelerator Generation with Control Flow and Data Access Optimization
problem: High-level synthesis for custom accelerators requires manual kernel selection and extraction, limiting automated SoC accelerator design; existing tools lack control flow and data access optimization.
method: Cayman uses hierarchical program representation to automatically select kernels with general control flows, specializes processor-accelerator interfaces for data access acceleration, and introduces accelerator merging to synthesize reusable accelerators.

title: Libra: A Hybrid-Sparse Attention Accelerator Featuring Multi-Level Workload Balance
problem: Transformer inference is bottlenecked by high computational complexity and memory usage; hybrid sparsity (value-level + bit-level) can improve efficiency but causes severe load imbalance across compute units, limiting actual acceleration benefits.
method: Libra combines algorithm-hardware co-design: algorithmically uses filtered bit-group sparsification (FBS) for structured weight sparsity and dynamic bit-group quantization (DBQ) for activation sparsification. Hardwareeside introduces task pool enabling multi-level workload balancing and adaptive bit-width architecture supporting simultaneous computations at varying bit-widths.

title: Look Before You Leap: A Self-Review Bayesian Optimization Method for Constrained High-Dimensional Design Space Exploration
problem: Parameterizable RISC-V processor design exploration faces high model errors during Bayesian optimization and lacks effective constraint handling for practical feasibility.
method: Proposes SRBO (Self-Review Bayesian Optimization) integrating teacher-student paradigm within local Bayesian optimization to reduce model errors; uses deep ensembles for effective constraint handling.

title: PacTrain: Pruning and Adaptive Sparse Gradient Compression for Efficient Collective Communication in Distributed Deep Learning
problem: Distributed DNN training is bottlenecked by gradient aggregation overhead; existing gradient compression schemes fail to accelerate training while preserving accuracy.
method: PacTrain actively prunes DNN weights (sparsifying gradients); performs lightweight adaptive compression using known global sparsity patterns; integrates with allreduce primitive for compatibility with distributed training frameworks.

title: AutoClock: Automated Clock Management for Power-Efficient HLS Designs on FPGAs
problem: FPGA high-level synthesis tools lack comprehensive clock management solutions; diverse clock resources create a large design space and multi-clock domain handling is inefficient, leading to suboptimal power consumption.
method: AutoClock is an integrated clock management framework that allocates clock resources, assigns modules to clock domains, addresses metastability and time-division multiplexing issues, and hierarchically gates clocks. The tool uses heuristics and constraint satisfaction to optimize clock domain assignments and gating.

title: Towards In-Situ Neuromorphic Computing Architecture for Event Stream Super-Resolution
problem: Event-based cameras generate sparse, low-resolution event streams mitigating motion blur in high-speed scenarios but lacking sufficient spatial resolution. Super-resolution of event streams requires efficient neuromorphic hardware architecture avoiding excessive intermediate storage.
method: Proposes spiking neural network (SNN) based accelerator with hardware-friendly designs: simplified neuron models, optimized convolutions, hierarchical parallel array. Novel Kernel-Channel-Timestamp-Row (KCTR) dataflow with dual-pipeline structure achieves in-situ computing, eliminating inter-layer spike storage.

title: ColumnDisturb: Understanding Column-based Read Disturbance in Real DRAM Chips and Implications for Future Systems
problem: A newly discovered DRAM read disturbance phenomenon called ColumnDisturb allows a single aggressor row activation to disturb DRAM cells through bitlines (columns), inducing bitflips in rows sharing the same columns across multiple subarrays — up to 3072 rows simultaneously in DDR4 — which is fundamentally different from RowHammer/RowPress that affect only a few adjacent rows in a single subarray.
method: The paper conducts a rigorous experimental characterization of ColumnDisturb on 216 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major DRAM manufacturers. Experiments vary temperature, data patterns, DRAM timing parameters (tRCD, tRAS, tRP), average bitline voltage, memory access patterns, and spatial variation across chips. The study measures minimum time to first bitflip, affected row count, and bitflip counts under nominal 63.6ms DDR4 refresh windows. The authors compare ColumnDisturb severity against DRAM retention failures and perform cycle-level simulation to quantify the impact on retention-aware refresh mechanisms that propose to skip refreshes for cells with long retention times.

title: IBM's Power11 Processor
problem: High-performance server and HPC workloads require next-generation processors with improved single-thread performance, power efficiency, and memory bandwidth.
method: IBM Power11 builds on the POWER ISA with enhanced core microarchitecture, improved cache hierarchy, memory controllers, and accelerators for specialized workloads.

title: ATiM: Autotuning Tensor Programs for Processing-in-DRAM
problem: Current software stacks for DRAM-PIM (specifically UPMEM) rely on hand-tuned libraries, lack high-level programming abstractions, and have no systematic optimization framework, making it difficult to achieve peak hardware utilization for tensor workloads including LLM layers.
method: ATiM is a search-based optimizing tensor compiler for the UPMEM DRAM-PIM architecture. It jointly searches the host-side and kernel-side tensor program space, applying PIM-aware optimizations to handle boundary conditions introduced by the banked DRAM layout. The compiler extends standard autotuning search algorithms to cover the expanded UPMEM-specific search space (e.g., tasklet counts, loop tiling, data placement across DPU banks), then generates fused, hardware-specific code without requiring manual library authoring.

title: BS-PDN-Last: Towards Optimal Power Delivery Network Design With Multifunctional Backside Metal Layers
problem: Backside metal layers in advanced chips can serve multiple functions (power delivery, signal routing, thermal); traditional PDN-first design flows reserve these layers for power, leaving suboptimal signal routing and performance trade-offs.
method: BS-PDN-last flow defers power routing to the post-signal routing stage, allowing signal routing to optimize for performance first, then power delivery networks to adapt to remaining backside resources. Uses vector-based IR-drop analysis for accurate power estimation.

title: CORDOBA: Carbon-Efficient Optimization Framework for Computing Systems
problem: Optimizing the carbon footprint of computing systems across large hardware design spaces is intractable with existing methods because it requires simultaneously trading off operational carbon, embodied carbon, performance, power, and area (PPA) under uncertainty in carbon intensity parameters.
method: CORDOBA introduces the total Carbon Delay Product (tCDP) metric — product of total lifecycle carbon (operational + embodied) and application execution time — as a single scalar objective for carbon-efficient hardware optimization. The framework performs design-space exploration by sweeping hardware configurations (e.g., core count, memory hierarchy, 2D vs. 3D integration via chiplet stacking) and evaluating tCDP under parametric uncertainty in carbon intensity, eliminating up to 98% of the design space as Pareto-dominated. Two case studies apply CORDOBA to real CPU systems: halving cores from 8 to 4 and adopting 3D-stacked logic+memory integration.

title: Ironwood: Delivering Best in Class perf, perf/TCO and perf/Watt for Reasoning Model Training and Serving
problem: Reasoning models (e.g., OpenAI o1, DeepSeek-R1) require massive compute for both training and inference with long-horizon thinking patterns; Ironwood targets optimal performance, TCO, and energy efficiency for this emerging workload class.
method: Ironwood likely combines enhanced memory bandwidth for extended compute/token reasoning traces, optimized matrix multiplication for reasoning compute patterns, and possibly novel interconnect/collective operation support tailored to reasoning model parallelization strategies.
